```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
options(poolinfo.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
pct <- function(x) round(100 * x)
has_metafor <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)
```

In a multisite trial each site gives an estimate of the intervention's
effect, with a standard error. A hierarchical model shrinks each estimate
toward the overall mean, a noisy site's estimate more than a precise
one's. poolinfo summarizes this shrinkage across all the sites of a trial.
The summaries are worth a look before you rank the sites, report their
effects or study how the effect varies among them, because they say how
much of each site's own estimate survives in the model's results, and
they bear on which estimator suits such a goal [@lee2026]. In this
vignette we analyze one outcome of a real trial, from the site estimates
to the report.

```{r library}
library(poolinfo)
```

## The data

The Online Credit Recovery Study randomized students who had failed
Algebra 1 or English 9 in their first year of high school to one of two
summer courses at their school, an online course or the school's usual
teacher-directed course [@rickles2024]. The data set `ocrs` has one row
for each of the `r nrow(ocrs)` school-by-subject sites in which students
were assigned to both courses.

```{r data}
head(ocrs[, c("site", "subject", "n", "estimate", "se")])
```

```{r data-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(nrow(ocrs) == 32L, min(ocrs$n) == 24L, max(ocrs$n) == 104L)
```

Each `estimate` is the effect of assignment to the online course on
passing the course, as a difference in proportions, and `se` is its
standard error. A negative estimate means that, in that site, a smaller
proportion of the students assigned to the online course passed. Within a
site, the estimate comes from a regression of passing on the assignment
indicator and the randomization blocks, so it weights the blocks
differently from a comparison of all the site's students. `?ocrs` gives
the details, and `vignette("multisite-trial")` compares this contrast with
other first-stage analyses.

## Fitting the posterior

`reliability_posterior()` takes the estimates and their standard errors.
We also record the scale of the effects and the estimand at each site,
which the printed output and the report sentences repeat.

```{r fit}
fit <- reliability_posterior(
  estimate, se = se, site = site, data = ocrs,
  scale_label = "risk difference",
  target_label = "the block-adjusted intention-to-treat contrast for course passing"
)
fit
```

```{r fit-facts, include = FALSE}
ps <- profile_summary(fit)
val <- function(q, col = "mean") ps[[col]][ps$quantity == q]
v <- ocrs$se^2
gm_se <- sqrt(exp(mean(log(v))))
ratio <- val("sigma_tau")^2 / gm_se^2
V <- val("V")
factor_se <- exp(sqrt(V) / 2)
lead_H <- val("I") * (1 - val("I")) * V / 2
lead_gap <- lead_H * (1 - 2 * val("I"))
gap <- plugin_gap(fit)
pairs <- sum(table(ocrs$school) == 2L)
stopifnot(
  all(fit$checks$status == "ok"),
  val("I", "lower") < 0.5, prob_above(fit) > 0.95,
  ratio > 1.8, ratio < 2.5,
  abs(lead_H - val("H")) < 0.002,
  sign(lead_gap) == sign(val("mean") - val("I")),
  val("mean") < val("I"), val("I") - val("mean") < 0.01,
  val("J_eff") > 31,
  all(gap$difference[1:2] > 0),
  val("effect_mean", "upper") < 0,
  abs(V - mean((log(v) - mean(log(v)))^2)) < 1e-12,
  pairs == 8L
)
if (has_metafor) {
  reml <- metafor::rma(estimate, sei = se, data = ocrs, method = "REML")
  I_reml <- reliability_profile(reml)$stats[["I"]]
  stopifnot(I_reml < val("I"), reml$I2 > 60, reml$I2 < 75)
}
```

We use flat priors on the mean and on the between-site standard
deviation $\sigma_\tau$, as @lee2026 does, and the posterior comes from
numerical integration over $\sigma_\tau$ in a fraction of a second. See
`vignette("posterior-summaries")` for other priors and how much they
matter. The last two lines of the header state an assumption and a
definition. The model treats the standard errors as exact, although they
are estimates too, so the posterior intervals leave out the uncertainty
in the standard errors themselves, and a different first-stage analysis
of the same trial could give different diagnostics. And each site counts
equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size, so a site of
`r min(ocrs$n)` students weighs as much as one of `r max(ocrs$n)`.

## Site reliabilities

Write $\hat\tau_j$ for site $j$'s estimate and $v_j$ for its sampling
variance, the squared standard error. Given $\sigma_\tau$ and the mean
$\mu$ of the effects, the posterior mean of site $j$'s effect is

$$
S_j \hat\tau_j + (1 - S_j)\mu, \qquad
S_j = \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j}.
$$

$S_j$ is the weight that the normal model puts on the site's own
estimate, and it is also the reliability of the site's estimate, the
proportion of the estimate's variance that comes from the true effects. We call the reliabilities
$S_1, \dots, S_J$ together the trial's reliability profile. @lee2026
writes $\sigma^2$ and $\tau$ for what this package calls $\sigma_\tau^2$
and $\mu$.

## The informativeness

The first summary of the profile is the *informativeness*,

$$
I = \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{\sigma_\tau^2 + \mathrm{GM}(v)},
$$

the reliability of a site whose sampling variance is the geometric mean
$\mathrm{GM}(v)$ of the $v_j$. It is also the mean of the reliabilities on
the logit scale [@lee2026], and @lee2025 use it to organize comparisons of
prior models and posterior summaries for site effects.

For course passing, the posterior mean of $I$ is `r num(val("I"))`, with a
95% posterior interval from `r num(val("I", "lower"))` to
`r num(val("I", "upper"))`. The geometric mean of the `r nrow(ocrs)`
standard errors is `r num(gm_se, 3)`, and the posterior mean of
$\sigma_\tau$ is `r num(val("sigma_tau"))`, so $\sigma_\tau^2$ is about
`r num(ratio, 1)` times $\mathrm{GM}(v)$. A site with the geometric-mean
standard error keeps about `r pct(val("I"))`% of its own estimate, which means that
the model moves its posterior mean about `r pct(1 - val("I"))`% of the way
toward the mean effect. The posterior probability that $I$ exceeds 1/2 is
`r num(prob_above(fit))`. At $I = 1/2$, $\sigma_\tau^2$ equals
$\mathrm{GM}(v)$ and a site with the geometric-mean standard error is
pulled halfway.

Meta-analysts will recognize the form of the $I^2$ statistic
[@higgins2002], which puts the "typical" sampling variance where $I$ puts
the geometric mean. `r if (has_metafor) sprintf("For these estimates, metafor's REML fit gives an $I^2$ of %s%%, and its estimate of $\\sigma_\\tau$, %s, is a little below the posterior mean.", round(reml$I2), num(sqrt(reml$tau2), 3))`

## How unequal the reliabilities are

The other three summaries describe how the reliabilities differ from site
to site, and all three depend on the logit variance $V$, the variance of
the logits of the reliabilities (with divisor $J$). Because
$\mathrm{logit}\, S_j = \log\sigma_\tau^2 - \log v_j$, $V$ is also the
variance of $\log v_j$, so the standard errors fix it. Here $V = `r num(V)`$, so the standard errors are typically within a
factor of `r num(factor_se)` of their geometric mean, although they range
from `r num(min(ocrs$se), 3)` to `r num(max(ocrs$se), 3)`.

The *mean reliability* $\bar S$ is the ordinary average of the $S_j$.
With $\sigma_\tau$ and $\mu$ known, the average posterior variance of the
site effects is $\sigma_\tau^2(1 - \bar S)$. In a trial whose sites all
had the geometric-mean standard error, every $S_j$ would equal $I$, so
$\bar S > I$ exactly when the site effects are estimated more precisely,
on average, than in that trial of equal precision. For passing, $\bar S$
is `r num(val("mean"))`, a little below $I$.

The *dispersion* $H$ measures how far the reliabilities are from one
another. Treat each $S_j$ as the success probability of a Bernoulli
distribution, a device for measuring how far apart reliabilities are
rather than a model for the data. Among constant values $p$, the average
Kullback-Leibler divergence
$J^{-1}\sum_j \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(p) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\}$ is
smallest at $p = I$, and $H$ is that smallest value. It is 0 only when all
the reliabilities are equal. When they are close to one another, the
leading terms in $V$ are

$$
H \approx \tfrac12 I(1 - I)V, \qquad
\bar S - I \approx \tfrac12 I(1 - I)(1 - 2I)V.
$$

The mean reliability is therefore usually below $I$ when $I > 1/2$ and
above it when $I < 1/2$, but a skewed profile, or a value of $I$ near 1/2,
can reverse the sign. `vignette("reliability-profiles")` shows when. For
passing, the leading term of $H$ at the posterior mean of $I$ is
`r num(lead_H, 3)`, close to $H$'s posterior mean of `r num(val("H"), 3)`.

The *concentration count*

$$
J_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{(\sum_j S_j)^2}{\sum_j S_j^2}
$$

describes how the total reliability $\sum_j S_j$ is shared among the
sites. It equals $J$ when every site has the same reliability, whatever
that reliability is, and it approaches 1 as one site comes to carry nearly
all of it. Its formula is Kish's, with the reliabilities as weights, but
it is not a sample size. It measures only how evenly the total is shared,
so sites that all have a reliability of 0.1 give $J$, and so do sites
that all have 0.9. For passing it is `r num(val("J_eff"), 1)` of
`r nrow(ocrs)`, so the total is shared almost evenly.

## The posterior in more detail

`summary()` adds the posterior standard deviations and medians, the
posterior of $\sigma_\tau$ and of the mean, and each diagnostic's value at
the posterior mean of $\sigma_\tau^2$.

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

The first block also gives the harmonic centroid, the harmonic mean of
the $S_j$, which equals $\sigma_\tau^2/(\sigma_\tau^2 + \bar v)$ with
$\bar v$ the arithmetic mean of the $v_j$, so it is never above $I$ or
$\bar S$. To use the numbers in your own code, `profile_summary()` returns
them as a data frame, one row per quantity.

```{r profile-summary}
print(profile_summary(fit), digits = 3)
```

```{r harmonic-facts, include = FALSE}
hm <- val("harmonic")
stopifnot(hm < val("mean"), hm < val("I"),
          abs(1 / mean(1 / site_reliability(se = ocrs$se, sigma_tau = 0.2)) -
                0.04 / (0.04 + mean(ocrs$se^2))) < 1e-12)
```

The mean effect has posterior mean
`r num(100 * val("effect_mean"), 1)` percentage points, with a 95%
posterior interval from `r num(100 * val("effect_mean", "lower"), 1)` to
`r num(100 * val("effect_mean", "upper"), 1)`. It is the mean of the
distribution of site effects, a mean over sites rather than students, so
it is not the effect for the average student. Because its interval lies
below 0, we conclude that assignment to the online course lowered passing
in the average site.

In the last block we compare each posterior mean with the diagnostic's
value at the posterior mean of $\sigma_\tau^2$, the number that a plug-in
of that estimate would report. $I$ and every $S_j$ are concave functions of
$\sigma_\tau^2$, so $I$ and $\bar S$ at the posterior mean of
$\sigma_\tau^2$ are never below their posterior means [@lee2026,
Proposition 3]. Here $I$ is `r num(gap$at_mean_sigma2[1], 3)` against
`r num(gap$posterior_mean[1], 3)`. $H$ and $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ have no
such order. `r if (has_metafor) sprintf("A plug-in of another estimate of $\\sigma_\\tau$ can fall on either side of the posterior mean: at metafor's REML estimate, $I$ is %s.", num(I_reml, 3))`

## Plots

`plot()` shows four panels: the estimates beside the posterior means of
the site effects, the sorted reliabilities, the posterior density of $I$,
and the analysis's position in the plane of $I$ and $V$. We multiply the
effects by 100 to show them in percentage points.

```{r dashboard, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 9, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Four panels: the site estimates and their posterior means with intervals; the sorted site reliabilities with the informativeness and its band; the posterior density of the informativeness; and the informativeness and logit variance plane."}
plot(fit, scale = 100)
```

In panel (a) we see the posterior means pulled toward the mean effect,
most visibly for the sites with wide intervals. Panel (b) shows the reliability
profile, from `r num(min(site_table(fit)$reliability))` to
`r num(max(site_table(fit)$reliability))`. In panel (d) the point lies
right of 1/2, where the leading term of $\bar S - I$ is negative, and
between the contours at 0.02 and 0.03 of $H$'s leading term. The plot is
a patchwork of ggplot objects. To change one panel, call its own function
(`plot_pooling()`, `plot_profile()`, `plot_functionals()` or
`plot_plane()`), which returns a ggplot object with a fuller caption.

## The sites

`site_table()` gives the numbers behind panels (a) and (b), one row per
site. We show the three sites with the largest standard errors and the
three with the smallest, in percentage points:

```{r sites}
sites <- site_table(fit)
sites <- sites[order(sites$se, decreasing = TRUE),
               c("site", "estimate", "se", "reliability", "effect")]
shown <- rbind(head(sites, 3), tail(sites, 3))
points <- c("estimate", "se", "effect")
shown[points] <- round(100 * shown[points], 1)
shown$reliability <- round(shown$reliability, 2)
shown
```

```{r site-facts, include = FALSE}
mu <- val("effect_mean")
move <- abs(sites$effect - sites$estimate) / abs(sites$estimate - mu)
stopifnot(max(abs(move - (1 - sites$reliability))) < 0.02,
          identical(sites$site[1:2], c("S24", "S14")))
```

Each posterior mean moves toward the mean effect by about $1 - S_j$ of the
distance between the site's estimate and the mean. A noisy site moves a
larger part of the way, but it moves far only if its estimate is far from
the mean. Site S24, with the largest standard error, moves
`r pct(1 - sites$reliability[1])`% of the way, from
`r num(100 * sites$estimate[1], 1)` to `r num(100 * sites$effect[1], 1)`
points. Site S14 is nearly as noisy and moves
`r pct(1 - sites$reliability[2])`% of the way, yet its estimate is close
to the mean, so its posterior mean changes by only
`r num(100 * abs(sites$effect[2] - sites$estimate[2]), 1)` points.

## Your own data

The same call works for any estimates with standard errors. You can give

- plain vectors, `reliability_posterior(y, se = s)`, or sampling variances
  with `se2`, such as the `vi` column that `metafor::escalc()` computes;
- a random-effects fit of metafor, `reliability_posterior(rma_fit)`, whose
  moderators become the mean model; `reliability_profile(rma_fit)` gives
  the profile at its REML estimate, and `vignette("meta-analysis")` works
  through an example;
- site covariates for the mean, `mean_model = ~ x`, so that each site is
  shrunk toward its predicted value;
- posterior draws of $\sigma_\tau$ from other software, to
  `reliability_draws()`, which also reads a brms fit of the form
  `y | se(sei) ~ 1 + (1 | site)` directly.

The model treats the sites as independent. In this trial `r pairs`
schools have a site in each subject, and some students appear in both.
We check how much that matters in `vignette("multisite-trial")`.

The model also gives every site the same mean and variance of the
effects, whatever its precision. When the smaller sites tend to have
larger effects, say, that common mean and variance can be inadequate
[@lee2026, Section 9]. A plot of the estimates against their standard
errors is a first check, although both are noisy:

```{r estimate-precision, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "The 32 site estimates for course passing plotted against their standard errors; the points show no trend."}
ggplot2::ggplot(ocrs, ggplot2::aes(x = se, y = estimate)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Standard error", y = "Site estimate") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

```{r precision-facts, include = FALSE}
r_se <- stats::cor(ocrs$estimate, ocrs$se)
stopifnot(abs(r_se) < 0.2)
```

In this trial the estimates show no trend with their standard errors (a
correlation of `r num(r_se)`). A trend would call for a covariate in the
mean model that carries it, or for a model in which the variance of the
effects depends on precision, which poolinfo does not fit.

## Reporting

@lee2026 recommends that a report

1. state the estimand at each site, its scale, the estimator and the
   standard errors;
2. give $I$ and $\bar S$ together, with $H$ or $V$;
3. add $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ when the concentration of the reliability
   matters.

`report_text()` writes the numbers as sentences, with the labels and the
conditioning on the standard errors. A report still needs to define the
four quantities and cite the paper.

```{r report}
writeLines(strwrap(report_text(fit, outcome = "course passing")))
```

`report_table()` gives the main numbers as a table, either as a data frame
or as markdown or LaTeX text. In an R Markdown document, a chunk with the
option `results = "asis"` turns the markdown into a table:

```{r report-table, results = "asis"}
cat(report_table(fit, format = "markdown"))
```

- `vignette("planning")` uses them to plan a trial.
- `vignette("implementation")` documents the computation.
